title: Identification of Sterol Responsive Elements in Human DNA Using Deep Learning
author: Davide Noto

steps.title: Extract TF peaks and SRE‑NFY couples
steps.instruction: Run the R script 1_extract_TF_peaks to read TF‑ChIP peak files, store positive peaks in ./pos and negative peaks in ./neg, select SRE and NFY peaks, keep only SRE‑NFY pairs that lie within 250 bp of each other, discard any negative peak that contains an SRE peak within 1000 bp, and write the positive couples to ENCODE_SREBF&NFY_peak.txt and the cleaned negatives to ENCODE_negative_peak.txt.

steps.title: Retrieve 500 bp sequences around peaks
steps.instruction: Execute the R script 2_retrieve_sequences_of_TF_peaks, which reads the two files created above, extracts a 500 bp DNA fragment centred on each peak, and saves the sequences in ./posseq for positives and ./negseq for negatives.

steps.title: Extract phylogenetic scores for positives
steps.instruction: Run the R script 3_extract_phylogenetic_matrices_for_positive_sequences; for every positive‑peak coordinate load the corresponding phyloP100way scores from the D:/chrs/Phylo wigFix files, and write a .phy file for each .seq file into the ./phylo subdirectory for later augmentation.

steps.title: Augment positive sequences
steps.instruction: Run the R script 4_augmentation_positive_sequences which creates up to 100 mutated copies of each ./posseq file. Mutations are introduced inversely to the phylogenetic score (highly conserved bases are mutated less often). Store the augmented files in ./augm with names ending in _[1..100].seq.

steps.title: Train CNN1D model on augmented data
steps.instruction: Execute the R script 5_DeepSRE6_train: load the CNN1D architecture from the SRE_models file with keras, use the custom DeepSRE6_generator to read each sequence, generate its reverse complement, concatenate forward and reverse, convert to a numerical matrix and one‑hot encode, feed batches of 512 samples to the model, fit in three successive stages with decreasing epoch numbers and an early‑stopping callback that halts a stage when no improvement is seen for a preset number of epochs, and finally save the best‑performing model as a .h5 file.

steps.title: Predict SRE‑NFY on promoter fragments
steps.instruction: Run the R script 6_DeepSRE6_evaluate: for every promoter in Deep_promoters (first 500 bp), generate overlapping 100‑bp fragments, pass each fragment through the trained model via the same generator to obtain a probability, collect all probabilities into a matrix and write to evalSRE7.csv, and flag promoters that contain at least three consecutive fragment probabilities greater than 0.9.

steps.title: Smooth fragment probabilities
steps.instruction: Execute the R script 7_smooth_promoter_probs: for each promoter’s probability list, slide a window of five consecutive values, discard the two extreme values, average the remaining three, move the window by one position, repeat until the end of the list, and store the smoothed series in averaged_mean_5_probs_SRE7.csv.

steps.title: Calculate GO‑term enrichment odds ratios
steps.instruction: Run the R script 8_DeepSRE6_calcORxGOterms: load promoter probabilities from evalSRE7.csv, GO term definitions from AllGOprocesslabel.csv, and gene‑to‑GO mappings from listGOterms_correct.txt (create this file if absent). Apply the three‑consecutive‑>0.9 rule to all promoters and write the resulting binary matrix to lethrmedia3prob09_full_stride10.csv. For each GO group, compare the number of promoters with the SRE‑NFY pattern to all other promoters using epitools::oddsratio.fisher, save odds ratios, confidence intervals and p‑values in OddsRatiosGoterms_f64k3_prox3prob09_full_strid10.csv, rank GO groups by decreasing odds ratio, analyse the top 30 groups in detail, and store the detailed results in ./GOgroups.

steps.title: Plot promoter analysis results
steps.instruction: Run the R script 9_DeepSRE6_plot_prom_results for a selected promoter (e.g., LSS): plot individual fragment probabilities as dots with a red line, overlay the smoothed probabilities (gray line), add blue bars for ENCODE SRE peaks, red bars for ENCODE NFY peaks, green bars for peaks used in model training, blue shaded bars for independent SRE peaks, and red shaded bars for independent NFY peaks, using data generated in previous steps.

steps.title: Occlusion analysis of promoter bases
steps.instruction: Execute the R script 10_DeepSRE6_promoter_occlusion: for each 500‑bp promoter, generate overlapping 100‑bp fragments, obtain the baseline probability for each fragment, then sequentially set each base to zero (occlude) and recompute the fragment probability, producing a list of 100 occlusion probabilities per fragment. Average the occlusion profiles across overlapping fragments position‑wise and plot the final importance curve for the whole promoter.

steps.title: Occlusion analysis of ENCODE peaks
steps.instruction: Run the R script 10b_DeepSRE6_ENCODEpeak_occlusion, which repeats the base‑occlusion procedure of step 10 on sequences stored in ./posseq (training peaks) and ./negseq (control peaks), storing the resulting importance profiles for each peak.

description: INTRODUCTION DeepSRE is a procedure that uses Deep Learning to identify possible SRE-NFY co-occurrence in gene promoters. The Deep Learning model consist of a Convolutional Neural Network 1-D model that is trained on SRE and NFY putative sequences contained in peaks identified by Transcription Factor Chromatin Immuno Precipitation (TF-ChIP) experiments. The peaks are identified by chromosomal coordinates listed in the ENCODE network database interrogated by the UCSC genome browser Table tool. The procedure do not represent a fully operational software, but it is a simple list of R language routines that must be executed sequentially within the Rstudio environment to produce the desired output. Working directories, working files requires by the procedures, are to be set manually, so an “a-priori” knowledge of R language and RStudio functionalities are also required. DeepSRE requires Reticulate, Keras and Tensorflow packages to work. Anaconda 3 was used to create a R python environment named “r-tensorflow”, that contains Tensorflow 1.14. The program has not been tested in Tensorflow 2.0. The complete procedure to install Keras and Tensorflow in RStudio is explained in the dedicated “R interface to Keras” site at https://keras.rstudio.com/. An intermediate knowledge of Keras is also suggested.
